clue.text: Bully was entering plea for some quiet bender

indicators.note: the word was goes inside the hush request, so 'entering' signals one piece put within another

parts.note: SH is the sound made to ask for quiet
taken as written
a buckler is one who buckles, that is bends something

explanation.surface: A bully barges in on someone begging for peace and quiet during a drinking spree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bender' suggests a drinking bout; here it is one who buckles (bends). WAS goes inside SH.
explanation.definitionFit: A swaggering, blustering adventurer was once a byword for a bragging ruffian or bully.

clue.text: Drink wine for sustenance

parts.note: to sup is to drink in small mouthfuls
port is a fortified wine from Portugal

explanation.surface: Someone turning to a glass of wine as their nourishment.
explanation.definitionFit: To give sustenance is to keep going or uphold; the two words are synonyms in the sense of maintenance.

clue.text: On such a night was Sinbad created

definitions.text: On such a night was Sinbad created

parts.words: On such a night was Sinbad created
parts.note: Sinbad the Sailor's tales belong to the collection known as the Thousand and One Nights, so the clue asks what kind of night bore him

explanation.walkthrough: The Arabian Nights is the familiar English title of the Thousand and One Nights, where Sinbad's voyages are told.
explanation.definitionFit: The story collection is called the Arabian Nights, so the nights in question are of that Middle Eastern kind.

clue.text: Epicureans who may be dishonest

indicators.note: the letters of the following word may be turned into the answer, so 'may be' asks for a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Pleasure-seekers who might well be untrustworthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May be' signals that DISHONEST can be rearranged into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Epicureans and their like are pleasure-seekers, devoted to enjoyment as life's chief good.

clue.text: Unqualified to speak

definitions.meaning: to say aloud or voice words

explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means total or complete; as a verb it means to give voice to words.

clue.text: They have a bloody tie in the race!

definitions.text: They have a bloody tie in the race!

parts.words: They have a bloody tie in the race!
parts.note: reads like competitors locked in a fierce dead heat, but a blood tie is family kinship and the race is the human family or a people

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tie' and 'race' suggest a sporting contest; they mean a family bond and a lineage.
explanation.definitionFit: Relatives by birth share a blood relationship within the same stock or people.

clue.text: Inspect main broken in river

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go inside the river's name

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, south-west England

indicators.note: something broken has its parts disordered, so the letters of main are rearranged

explanation.surface: Checking a water main that has burst into a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken' makes AMIN from MAIN, and 'in' puts it inside EXE, the Devon river.
explanation.definitionFit: To inspect something is to scrutinise it closely, a direct synonym.

clue.text: " This batter'd —— Whose Portals are alternate Night and Day " (Fitzgerald)

definitions.text: This batter'd —— Whose Portals are alternate Night and Day " (Fitzgerald)

parts.words: This batter'd —— Whose Portals are alternate Night and Day
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Edward Fitzgerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, which likens the world to a worn wayside inn

explanation.walkthrough: The missing word comes from Fitzgerald's Rubaiyat: the world is a battered inn whose doors are day and night.
explanation.definitionFit: The word for an eastern inn for travelling caravans fills the gap in the quoted line, the image for the world.

clue.text: Generally handy to express approval thus

definitions.text: Generally handy to express approval thus

parts.words: Generally handy to express approval thus
parts.note: showing approval is usually done with the hands, by clapping them together

explanation.definitionFit: Clapping one's hands is the usual way to show approval, which is what this word means.

clue.text: Man is subject to its laws

definitions.text: Man is subject to its laws

parts.words: Man is subject to its laws
parts.note: Man here is the Isle of Man, whose own parliament makes its laws, not mankind in general

explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' seems to be humanity; it is the Isle of Man, a self-governing island between Britain and Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The parliament of the Isle of Man passes the island's laws, so its people are subject to them.

clue.text: But not how children should behave on breaking-up day

definitions.text: But not how children should behave on breaking-up day

parts.words: But not how children should behave on breaking-up day
parts.note: breaking-up day is the last day of a British school term; the clue plays on a word for breaking up that children should not do literally

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain schools 'break up' for the holidays; the answer means to fall to pieces, which pupils should not do.
explanation.definitionFit: To fall apart into fragments is to break up, the literal sense of the school phrase.

clue.text: In the old mode, this sort of harp?

definitions.meaning: one of the old church modes in music, corresponding to the natural minor scale
a harp strung so that wind passing over it makes it sound

explanation.definitionFit: It names both a medieval musical mode and a wind harp, after the Greek god of the winds.

clue.text: What's left of engineers' power suppliers

parts.note: RE stands for the Royal Engineers of the British Army
the mains supply electricity to buildings

explanation.surface: The leftovers of the engineers' electricity cables.
explanation.definitionFit: Leftovers or a residue are what stays behind after the rest is gone.

clue.text: Bill with some weight in London

parts.note: Bill gives AC
a ton is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A heavyweight piece of legislation going through Parliament in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: ACTON is a district of west London.
explanation.definitionFit: A suburb of west London, so it is a place found within the capital.

clue.text: Number observed taking in what's happening

indicators.note: one word takes the other into its middle, so 'taking in' signals a container

parts.note: something observed has been seen
an event is something that happens

explanation.surface: Someone noticing a figure while watching proceedings.
explanation.definitionFit: Ten plus seven is a whole number.

clue.text: Possibly saves a lag from servitude

indicators.note: possibly says these letters could be arranged otherwise, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Perhaps someone rescues an old convict from slavery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lag' is British slang for a convict.
explanation.definitionFit: Being a feudal dependant meant subjection to a lord, a state of bondage.

clue.text: We don't expect them on French spires anyway

parts.note: sur is French for on

indicators.note: taking the letters in any order signals a rearrangement of the word spires

explanation.surface: Unexpected sights on top of church steeples in France.
explanation.definitionFit: Unexpected events are by nature the things nobody sees coming.

clue.text: Practised penmanship below (say) the Round House?

indicators.note: say signals the words are to be spoken, giving a sound-alike

parts.note: practised penmanship is wrote and below is under, so the phrase gives wrote under

explanation.surface: Someone did their handwriting exercises beneath a famous circular building.
explanation.walkthrough: WROTE UNDER, said in a non-rhotic British accent, sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A domed circular building is a round house, defined by example, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Sums returned by boxing arbitrator and German second

parts.note: the referee in a boxing ring, shortened to ref
und is German for and

explanation.surface: Money paid back by a boxing referee and a German assistant.
explanation.definitionFit: Money paid back to a customer is a repayment, sums given back.

clue.text: Obliterate article in Gaelic

indicators.note: the article sits in the word for Gaelic

parts.note: Erse is an old name for Scottish or Irish Gaelic
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Censoring a piece of writing in the Gaelic language.
explanation.definitionFit: To wipe out or rub out completely is to obliterate.

clue.text: What Browning's love does to him ? Never!

definitions.text: What Browning's love does to him ? Never!

parts.words: What Browning's love does to him ? Never!
parts.note: alludes to Robert Browning's poem Life in a Love, which opens 'Escape me? Never, beloved!'

explanation.walkthrough: Browning's poem opens with the lover asking whether his beloved could get away from him, and answering 'Never'.
explanation.definitionFit: The beloved in the poem tries to get away from the speaker, which the poet declares will never happen.

clue.text: Jack and Mark take the pledge

parts.note: a jack is a sailor, and AB is able-bodied seaman
a stain is a mark

explanation.surface: Two men, Jack and Mark, swear off drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' and 'Mark' look like names; they are a sailor and a blemish. To take the pledge is to vow to give up alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking the pledge means vowing to refrain from alcohol, which is to refrain or hold back.

clue.text: Biscuit cooked at a fair

indicators.note: cooked suggests the letters are made into something new, so rearrange at a fair

explanation.surface: A biscuit baked at a fairground.
explanation.definitionFit: An almond-flavoured macaroon-like biscuit is named after the almond liqueur.

clue.text: Crime for which a priest is beheaded

indicators.note: the priest loses his head, so the first letter of the word is cut off

parts.note: a parson is a parish priest

explanation.surface: An offence for which a clergyman is executed.
explanation.definitionFit: Deliberately setting fire to property is a criminal offence.

clue.text: Nobody's fault if his charges are unreasonable

definitions.text: Nobody's fault if his charges are unreasonable

parts.words: Nobody's fault if his charges are unreasonable
parts.note: charges sounds like fees, but they are accusations, and if they are unfounded the blame lies with no one but the person making them

explanation.definitionFit: One who brings charges against someone else is a complainant or prosecutor.

clue.text: Local gins in variety for the cricketing period

parts.note: a local is a British pub, so an inn

indicators.note: putting the letters of gins in variety means changing their order

explanation.surface: A pub serves gin in many flavours during the cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' is British for one's neighbourhood pub. In cricket, a side's turn to bat is its innings.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, each team's turn at batting is a distinct period of play.

clue.text: Anglo Scottish Petroleum shortly to stop supply of road material

parts.note: shortly means abbreviated, so the company name becomes its initials
a halt is a stop

explanation.surface: An oil company is about to cut off deliveries of road-surfacing material.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarmac-like bitumen mixture is the material used to surface roads.

clue.text: Christian whose emperor was non-suited

parts.note: Christian is the middle name of the Danish storyteller who wrote The Emperor's New Clothes, in which the ruler parades unclothed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Christian' looks like a believer; it is a middle name. 'Non-suited' puns on a legal nonsuit and wearing no suit.
explanation.definitionFit: The Danish fairytale writer, middle name Christian, wrote of an emperor fooled into wearing nothing.
